title: The Puratan tradition
hook: one old family of janamsakhis, valued by historians for its early material

segments.voice: Yesterday, the janamsakhis: books of Guru Nanak's life-stories, in several traditions. Your line was stories that carry truth.

An old house, renovated many times. New kitchen, new windows, a porch someone added. But go down to the basement and there's a stretch of stone wall, rough and uneven, from when the house was first built. A builder will run a hand along it and say: that's the original. Everything else rests on it. There isn't one janamsakhi but several families of them, and historians go looking for the stone wall in the basement. Today: Puratan.
screen: `AN OLD HOUSE, RENOVATED.` → `ROUGH STONE IN THE BASEMENT.` → `THAT'S THE ORIGINAL.`

segments.voice: Puratan is a Punjabi word for old. This family of janamsakhis carries that name, the old ones, and historians value it for its early material about Guru Nanak's life. It isn't one book with one author. It's a group of related manuscripts telling the stories in much the same way. Some readers describe it as plainer than later tellings. The stories are spare and move quickly, with less decoration around them, and the Guru's own hymns are woven into the scenes. Take the river story, one of the pictures from yesterday's opening. Nanak goes down to the river to bathe and doesn't come back. His family and friends search, and fear the worst. When he returns, the Puratan tradition has him say: there is no Hindu, there is no Musalman. Sikh teachers often explain those words as a call to look past the labels people fight over, toward the One who made them all, not a rejection of anyone's faith. A historian reading that story isn't trying to disprove it. They're asking a different question: which parts of the telling are oldest, closest to the people who knew Nanak, and which grew around it later? The Puratan tradition is where historians often start that work. And calling something the old telling doesn't make the later tellings worthless. A renovated house is still a home. But when you want to know how the house began, you go to the stone.
screen: `PURATAN: OLD.` · `A FAMILY OF MANUSCRIPTS, NOT ONE BOOK.` · `PLAIN, SPARE, HYMNS WOVEN IN.` · `WHERE HISTORIANS START.` · then, large: `THE OLD TELLING.`

segments.voice: Choose someone you've known a long time, a parent, a friend, a place you've lived, and go past everything you know about them today, back to the very first picture you have: where you stood, the light, what was said. That first picture is the stone wall; notice how much has been built on it since, and that it's still there, holding it up. If you pray, you can say Waheguru when you reach it.
Puratan, the old family of janamsakhis, plain and spare, where historians look for early material about Guru Nanak's life.
Your line: the old telling. Later tellings rest on it too. Day seven hundred twenty-three, done.

howItsDone: Scholars of Sikh history read the Puratan janamsakhis alongside other traditions, while gurdwara teachers draw sakhis such as the river story from them for katha and for children.
